FP512 MCQ Practice — CFP Study Lab
==================================
FP512 — Risk Management, Insurance & Employee Benefits
===== FP512 MCQ PRACTICE =====

Read the question and options, commit to an answer, then turn the page for the correct choice, the explanation, and why each wrong option is wrong.
83 questions · 8 sections.



===== FP512 · M1 PRINCIPLES OF INSURANCE =====

[16 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 16 · Risk Principles]
Which type of risk is generally insurable?
A. Speculative risk
B. Dynamic risk
C. Pure risk
D. Fundamental dynamic risk
Answer: C. Pure risk
Pure risk involves only the chance of loss or no loss (no chance of gain) and is insurable. Speculative and dynamic risks are not insurable.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Speculative risk — Speculative risk has both loss AND gain potential (like gambling/investing), so it is uninsurable.
✗ Dynamic risk — Dynamic risks arise from economy-wide changes and are not insurable; only pure risk is.
✗ Fundamental dynamic risk — Combines two uninsurable categories; insurers cover pure, particular risks, not fundamental/dynamic ones.

——————————
[Q 2 / 16 · Risk Principles]
A homeowner faces a low-frequency but high-severity exposure (e.g., a house fire). Per the risk management matrix, the most appropriate technique is to:
A. Retain the risk
B. Transfer the risk
C. Avoid the activity
D. Reduce the activity
Answer: B. Transfer the risk
Low frequency/high severity exposures are best transferred via insurance. High frequency/high severity calls for avoidance or reduction; low/low calls for retention.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Retain the risk — Retention fits low-frequency/low-severity losses you can absorb, not a catastrophic house fire.
✗ Avoid the activity — Avoidance is for high-frequency/high-severity exposures; you cannot practically 'avoid' owning a home.
✗ Reduce the activity — Reduction suits high-frequency exposures; a rare but severe loss is best transferred to an insurer.

——————————
[Q 3 / 16 · Risk Principles]
Which is NOT one of the four elements of an insurable risk from the insurer's perspective?
A. A large number of homogeneous exposure units
B. The loss must be definite and measurable
C. The loss must be catastrophic to the insurer
D. The loss must be fortuitous
Answer: C. The loss must be catastrophic to the insurer
An insurable loss must NOT be catastrophic to the insurer. The other three are required elements.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ A large number of homogeneous exposure units — This IS a required element (law of large numbers), so it is not the exception.
✗ The loss must be definite and measurable — This IS a required element, so it is not the exception.
✗ The loss must be fortuitous — A fortuitous (accidental/unexpected) loss IS required, so it is not the exception.

——————————
[Q 4 / 16 · Insurable Interest]
For property and casualty insurance, when must insurable interest exist?
A. Only when the policy is issued
B. Only at the time of loss
C. At both policy issue and at the time of loss
D. Insurable interest is not required for P&C
Answer: C. At both policy issue and at the time of loss
P&C insurable interest must exist both at issue and at the time of loss. For life insurance it need exist only when the policy is issued.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Only when the policy is issued — That is the LIFE insurance rule; for P&C, insurable interest must also exist at the time of loss.
✗ Only at the time of loss — P&C requires insurable interest both at issue and at loss, not solely at loss.
✗ Insurable interest is not required for P&C — P&C absolutely requires insurable interest to prevent wagering and enforce indemnity.

——————————
[Q 5 / 16 · Insurance Limits]
A peril, the cause of a loss, is best illustrated by:
A. A frayed electrical cord
B. A fire
C. An icy sidewalk
D. Storing gasoline indoors
Answer: B. A fire
A peril is the cause of loss (fire). The frayed cord, icy sidewalk, and stored gasoline are hazards that increase the chance of loss.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ A frayed electrical cord — A frayed cord is a physical HAZARD that increases the chance of loss, not the peril itself.
✗ An icy sidewalk — Icy conditions are a hazard raising the likelihood of a fall, not the direct cause (peril) of loss.
✗ Storing gasoline indoors — Storing gasoline is a hazard that increases loss potential, not a peril.

——————————
[Q 6 / 16 · Insurance Regulation]
The McCarran-Ferguson Act of 1945 established that insurance is primarily regulated by:
A. The federal government
B. The states
C. The NAIC directly
D. The courts only
Answer: B. The states
McCarran-Ferguson (Public Law 15) reserved most insurance regulation to the states, while reserving areas like antitrust to the federal government.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ The federal government — McCarran-Ferguson reserved most insurance regulation to the STATES, not the federal government.
✗ The NAIC directly — The NAIC only develops model laws; it has no direct regulatory authority—states regulate.
✗ The courts only — Regulation is legislative/administrative at the state level, not conducted solely by courts.

——————————
[Q 7 / 16 · Insurance Contract Law]
An insurance contract drafted by the insurer that the insured must accept or reject without negotiation is characterized as a contract of:
A. Adhesion
B. Indemnity
C. Aleatory exchange
D. Subrogation
Answer: A. Adhesion
A contract of adhesion is prepared by one party (the insurer) on an accept-or-reject basis. Aleatory refers to chance; indemnity is a principle, not a characteristic.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Indemnity — Indemnity is the principle of restoring pre-loss position, not the take-it-or-leave-it drafting characteristic.
✗ Aleatory exchange — Aleatory refers to unequal exchange based on chance, not the one-sided drafting of the contract.
✗ Subrogation — Subrogation is the insurer's right to pursue a third party after paying a claim, not a contract type.

——————————
[Q 8 / 16 · Insurance Contract Law]
Which form of insurance is the principal exception to the principle of indemnity?
A. Homeowners insurance
B. Auto collision insurance
C. Life insurance
D. Commercial property insurance
Answer: C. Life insurance
Life insurance pays a stated face/death benefit rather than restoring a pre-loss financial position, making it the exception to indemnity.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Homeowners insurance — Homeowners follows indemnity—it restores the insured's pre-loss position, subject to policy limits.
✗ Auto collision insurance — Collision coverage is an indemnity contract, paying actual cash value or repair cost, not a set face amount.
✗ Commercial property insurance — Commercial property is indemnity-based, reimbursing actual loss rather than a stated benefit.

——————————
[Q 9 / 16 · Liability & Torts]
Which is NOT one of the four elements required to prove negligence?
A. A duty is owed
B. The duty was breached
C. Actual damages occurred
D. The act was intentional
Answer: D. The act was intentional
Negligence is an unintentional tort. Its four elements are duty owed, duty breached, actual damages, and proximate cause.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ A duty is owed — Duty owed IS one of the four elements, so it is not the exception.
✗ The duty was breached — Breach of duty IS a required element, so it is not the exception.
✗ Actual damages occurred — Actual damages IS a required element, so it is not the exception.

——————————
[Q 10 / 16 · Liability & Torts]
Under a pure contributory negligence rule, an injured plaintiff who was partly at fault will:
A. Recover damages reduced by their percentage of fault
B. Be barred from any recovery
C. Recover full damages
D. Recover only medical costs
Answer: B. Be barred from any recovery
Under contributory negligence, ANY negligence by the injured party bars recovery. Comparative negligence instead reduces recovery by the plaintiff's share of fault.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Recover damages reduced by their percentage of fault — That describes COMPARATIVE negligence; pure contributory bars recovery entirely for any plaintiff fault.
✗ Recover full damages — Any fault by the plaintiff bars recovery under contributory negligence—no full recovery.
✗ Recover only medical costs — Contributory negligence bars all recovery for a partly-at-fault plaintiff, not just non-medical damages.

——————————
[Q 11 / 16 · Agency]
An agent's authority that arises because it is necessary to transact business (such as collecting premiums), though not expressly stated, is:
A. Express authority
B. Implied authority
C. Apparent authority
D. Ratified authority
Answer: B. Implied authority
Implied authority is assumed as necessary to carry out the business of the agency. Express is stated in the contract; apparent is based on appearances to the client.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Express authority — Express authority is what is specifically WRITTEN in the agency contract, not what is merely necessary.
✗ Apparent authority — Apparent authority is based on how things appear to a third party, not on business necessity.
✗ Ratified authority — Ratification is after-the-fact approval of an unauthorized act, not authority necessary to do business.

——————————
[Q 12 / 16 · Agency]
An insurance broker legally represents:
A. The insurer
B. The insurance buyer
C. The NAIC
D. Both parties equally
Answer: B. The insurance buyer
A broker represents the insurance buyer (prospective insured) and cannot bind the insurer.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ The insurer — That describes an agent; a broker represents the buyer and cannot bind the insurer.
✗ The NAIC — The NAIC is a regulatory association; a broker represents the insurance buyer.
✗ Both parties equally — A broker owes its duty to the buyer, not equally to both sides.

——————————
[Q 13 / 16 · Underwriting]
A client who is careless because "it's insured anyway" exhibits a:
A. Moral hazard
B. Morale hazard
C. Physical peril
D. Speculative risk
Answer: B. Morale hazard
Morale hazard is indifference or carelessness because losses are insured. Moral hazard involves unethical conduct or misrepresentation.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Moral hazard — Moral hazard involves dishonesty/fraud (e.g., faking a claim); mere carelessness because it's insured is a MORALE hazard.
✗ Physical peril — Carelessness is an attitude, not a physical cause of loss; and 'peril' is a cause, not a hazard.
✗ Speculative risk — Speculative risk involves chance of gain or loss; this is a hazard describing insured indifference.

——————————
[Q 14 / 16 · Insurer Ratings]
Which rating agency is the oldest and specializes only in rating insurance companies?
A. Standard & Poor's
B. Moody's
C. A.M. Best
D. Fitch Ratings
Answer: C. A.M. Best
A.M. Best is the oldest agency and the only one specializing in insurance ratings; its top rating is A++ (Superior).
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Standard & Poor's — S&P rates many types of debt and firms broadly, not solely insurers, and is not the oldest insurance-specific rater.
✗ Moody's — Moody's is a general credit-rating agency, not the insurance-only specialist; A.M. Best is.
✗ Fitch Ratings — Fitch is a broad credit-rating agency and the youngest of the majors, not the insurance-only specialist.

——————————
[Q 15 / 16 · Liability & Torts]
Which type of damages awarded in a liability lawsuit is generally NOT insurable?
A. Special (economic) damages
B. General (pain and suffering) damages
C. Punitive damages
D. Compensatory damages
Answer: C. Punitive damages
Punitive damages punish reckless or intentional wrongdoing; insuring them would defeat that purpose, so most states treat them as uninsurable. Special and general damages are compensatory and are covered by liability policies.

——————————
[Q 16 / 16 · Insurer Ratings]
Which factor is a criterion for selecting an insurance COMPANY rather than an insurance agent?
A. Competence
B. Financial strength
C. Inclination to service the account
D. Experience and training
Answer: B. Financial strength
Financial strength (e.g., A.M. Best ratings) evaluates the insurance company. An agent is judged on competence, inclination to service, experience, training, and reputation.



===== FP512 · M2 PROPERTY & CASUALTY =====

[12 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 12 · Homeowners]
Under a homeowners policy, Coverage D provides:
A. Coverage for the dwelling
B. Coverage for detached structures
C. Loss-of-use coverage while the home is uninhabitable
D. Medical payments to others
Answer: C. Loss-of-use coverage while the home is uninhabitable
Coverage D is loss of use, covering additional living expenses while the dwelling is uninhabitable due to a covered peril.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Coverage for the dwelling — That is Coverage A (dwelling), not Coverage D.
✗ Coverage for detached structures — Detached/other structures are Coverage B, not Coverage D.
✗ Medical payments to others — Medical payments to others is Coverage F, not Coverage D (loss of use).

——————————
[Q 2 / 12 · Homeowners]
Which homeowners form is the most widely purchased and provides open perils on the dwelling but named perils on personal property?
A. HO-2
B. HO-3
C. HO-4
D. HO-8
Answer: B. HO-3
HO-3 (Special Form) is the most popular: open perils on real property, named perils on personal property.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ HO-2 — HO-2 (Broad Form) is named-perils on BOTH dwelling and contents, not open-perils on the dwelling.
✗ HO-4 — HO-4 is the renters/tenants form covering contents only, with no dwelling coverage.
✗ HO-8 — HO-8 is the modified/older-home form using actual cash value, not the popular open-peril HO-3.

——————————
[Q 3 / 12 · Homeowners]
A renter who wants coverage for personal property, liability, and loss of use (but not the building) should buy:
A. HO-3
B. HO-4
C. HO-6
D. HO-8
Answer: B. HO-4
HO-4 is the Contents Broad (Tenants/Renters) form, providing contents, liability, and loss of use with no Coverage A or B.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ HO-3 — HO-3 insures the dwelling (Coverages A/B), which a renter does not own and does not need.
✗ HO-6 — HO-6 is for condo unit-owners (includes limited building/interior coverage), not renters.
✗ HO-8 — HO-8 is the modified form for older homes the owner occupies, not a renters/tenants policy.

——————————
[Q 4 / 12 · Homeowners]
Under standard homeowners policies, Coverage C (personal property) is typically what percentage of Coverage A?
A. 10%
B. 25%
C. 50%
D. 80%
Answer: C. 50%
Coverage C is generally 50% of the dwelling (Coverage A) limit; Coverage B (other structures) is generally 10%.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 10% — 10% is the typical Coverage B (other structures) limit, not Coverage C.
✗ 25% — 25%–30% is a common Coverage D (loss of use) figure, not Coverage C, which is 50%.
✗ 80% — 80% is the coinsurance requirement for full replacement-cost recovery, not the Coverage C limit.

——————————
[Q 5 / 12 · Homeowners]
To have partial losses paid in full, a homeowner must insure the dwelling for at least what percentage of replacement cost?
A. 50%
B. 70%
C. 80%
D. 100%
Answer: C. 80%
The 80% coinsurance rule requires insuring at least 80% of replacement cost; otherwise partial losses are paid at the greater of ACV or the coinsurance-penalty formula.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 50% — Too low; the coinsurance requirement for full partial-loss payment is 80% of replacement cost.
✗ 70% — Not the standard threshold; the 80% coinsurance rule governs partial-loss recovery.
✗ 100% — Full replacement value isn't required for partial losses—80% satisfies the coinsurance rule (100% is needed to avoid any gap on total losses).

——————————
[Q 6 / 12 · Homeowners]
A home costs $400,000 to rebuild but is insured for only $300,000, with a $1,000 deductible. A covered partial loss is $20,000. Using the coinsurance penalty formula, the insurer pays:
A. $20,000
B. $18,750
C. $17,750
D. $15,000
Answer: C. $17,750
Required insurance = 80% × $400,000 = $320,000. ($300,000 ÷ $320,000) × $20,000 = $18,750, minus the $1,000 deductible = $17,750.

——————————
[Q 7 / 12 · Flood Insurance]
The predominant provider of residential flood insurance is:
A. Private insurers through the HO-3
B. The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)
C. The California Earthquake Authority
D. Lloyd's of London
Answer: B. The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)
Flood is excluded from standard HO policies; the federal government's NFIP is the predominant provider, often required by mortgage lenders in flood zones.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Private insurers through the HO-3 — Flood is EXCLUDED from HO-3 and all standard homeowners forms, so it isn't provided this way.
✗ The California Earthquake Authority — The CEA covers earthquakes in California, not flood insurance.
✗ Lloyd's of London — Lloyd's writes specialty/surplus lines but is not the predominant U.S. residential flood provider; the NFIP is.

——————————
[Q 8 / 12 · Personal Liability]
Coverage F (medical payments to others) under a homeowners policy:
A. Requires proof of negligence by the insured
B. Pays for injury to household members
C. Pays for injury to a non-resident without requiring negligence
D. Covers the insured's own medical bills
Answer: C. Pays for injury to a non-resident without requiring negligence
Coverage F pays for injury to a non-resident at the residence regardless of negligence. Household members cannot collect under it.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Requires proof of negligence by the insured — Coverage F pays regardless of fault—no proof of negligence is needed (that's the Coverage E liability standard).
✗ Pays for injury to household members — Coverage F excludes the insured's own household/resident family members; it covers non-residents.
✗ Covers the insured's own medical bills — Coverage F pays medical bills of OTHERS, not the insured's own injuries.

——————————
[Q 9 / 12 · Umbrella Policy]
A personal liability umbrella policy (PLUP) typically:
A. Replaces the homeowners and auto policies
B. Has a limit of at least $1 million and pays after underlying limits are exhausted
C. Pays before the homeowners and auto policies
D. Covers only the insured's medical bills
Answer: B. Has a limit of at least $1 million and pays after underlying limits are exhausted
A PLUP (catastrophe liability) typically has a limit of at least $1 million; the underlying HO/auto policy pays first, then the umbrella pays the difference.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Replaces the homeowners and auto policies — An umbrella supplements, not replaces, the underlying HO/auto policies, which must stay in force.
✗ Pays before the homeowners and auto policies — The umbrella pays only AFTER the underlying HO/auto limits are exhausted, not first.
✗ Covers only the insured's medical bills — A PLUP provides broad excess LIABILITY coverage, not the insured's own medical costs.

——————————
[Q 10 / 12 · Auto Insurance]
Which Personal Auto Policy coverage is mandatory in essentially all states?
A. Medical payments (Part B)
B. Liability (Part A)
C. Uninsured motorist (Part C)
D. Collision (Part D)
Answer: B. Liability (Part A)
Liability coverage (Part A) is the only mandatory part of the PAP; states have financial responsibility laws.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Medical payments (Part B) — Med-pay is optional first-party coverage, not the mandatory part; liability is.
✗ Uninsured motorist (Part C) — UM is required in some states but not essentially all; liability (Part A) is the universal requirement.
✗ Collision (Part D) — Collision is optional (often lender-required), not state-mandated; liability is the mandatory coverage.

——————————
[Q 11 / 12 · Auto Insurance]
In the auto split limit 25/50/10, the "50" represents:
A. Bodily injury per person
B. Bodily injury per accident
C. Property damage per accident
D. The deductible
Answer: B. Bodily injury per accident
25/50/10 means $25,000 bodily injury per person / $50,000 bodily injury per accident / $10,000 property damage.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Bodily injury per person — That is the first number (25) — the per-person BI cap, not the middle number.
✗ Property damage per accident — That is the last number (10), not the middle figure.
✗ The deductible — Split limits express liability caps, not a deductible; the deductible applies to your own collision/comprehensive.

——————————
[Q 12 / 12 · Auto Insurance]
Damage to your auto from hitting a deer would be covered under:
A. Collision
B. Comprehensive (other-than-collision)
C. Liability
D. Uninsured motorist
Answer: B. Comprehensive (other-than-collision)
Contact with a bird or animal falls under comprehensive (other-than-collision) coverage, along with fire, theft, vandalism, and glass breakage.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Collision — Collision covers impact with another vehicle or object; contact with an animal is specifically classified as other-than-collision.
✗ Liability — Liability pays others for damage you cause, not damage to your own auto.
✗ Uninsured motorist — UM applies when an at-fault uninsured driver injures you, not an animal strike.



===== FP512 · M3 LIFE INSURANCE =====

[15 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 15 · Life Insurance Types]
Which life insurance type guarantees the premium, death benefit, and cash value?
A. Annually renewable term
B. Universal life
C. Whole life
D. Variable life
Answer: C. Whole life
Whole life guarantees all three. Term has no cash value, UL's cash value is not guaranteed, and VL's cash value varies with the separate account.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Annually renewable term — Term has no cash value and its premium rises each year, so it guarantees none of the three.
✗ Universal life — UL's cash value is not guaranteed (interest-sensitive) and premiums are flexible.
✗ Variable life — VL's cash value varies with the separate-account subaccounts, so it is not guaranteed.

——————————
[Q 2 / 15 · Life Insurance Types]
A single-premium whole life policy is always classified as a:
A. Term policy
B. Modified endowment contract (MEC)
C. Nonqualified annuity
D. Group policy
Answer: B. Modified endowment contract (MEC)
A single premium exceeds the 7-pay limit, so single-premium life is always a MEC. Once a MEC, always a MEC.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Term policy — Whole life is permanent with cash value; single-premium funding does not make it term.
✗ Nonqualified annuity — It is life insurance, not an annuity — different tax and contract rules.
✗ Group policy — Single-premium whole life is an individual contract, unrelated to group status.

——————————
[Q 3 / 15 · Universal Life]
Under UL Option B (increasing death benefit), the death benefit equals:
A. The cash value only
B. The net amount at risk only
C. The net amount at risk plus the cash value
D. A level face amount
Answer: C. The net amount at risk plus the cash value
Option B pays NAR + cash value (an increasing benefit), keeping NAR level. Option A is level, with NAR decreasing as cash value grows.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ The cash value only — The death benefit is NAR plus cash value, not cash value alone.
✗ The net amount at risk only — Option B adds the cash value on top of the NAR, not NAR by itself.
✗ A level face amount — That describes Option A (level death benefit); Option B increases as cash value grows.

——————————
[Q 4 / 15 · Life Insurance Types]
Which policy lets the owner direct cash value into subaccounts and requires a prospectus?
A. Whole life
B. Universal life
C. Variable universal life
D. Limited-pay life
Answer: C. Variable universal life
Variable universal life uses a separate account with policyowner-directed subaccounts and must be sold with a prospectus. UL does not let the owner direct investments.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Whole life — Whole life has a fixed general-account cash value the owner cannot direct; no prospectus.
✗ Universal life — UL is interest-sensitive but does not let the owner pick subaccounts and needs no prospectus.
✗ Limited-pay life — Limited-pay is just whole life paid up early — no separate account, no prospectus.

——————————
[Q 5 / 15 · Equity-Indexed UL]
An EIUL has a 70% participation rate and the index gains 10%. What interest is credited?
A. 10%
B. 7%
C. 70%
D. 3%
Answer: B. 7%
A 70% participation rate credits 70% of the 10% gain = 7%. A rate cap would separately limit the maximum credited amount.

——————————
[Q 6 / 15 · Life Policy Provisions]
Under the incontestability clause, an insurer generally may not contest a policy after:
A. 6 months
B. 1 year in all states
C. No more than 2 years
D. 5 years
Answer: C. No more than 2 years
The incontestability period is no more than 2 years (1 year in some states). Fraud may have no statute of limitations.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 6 months — Far too short; the standard period is up to 2 years.
✗ 1 year in all states — One year applies in only some states, not all — the maximum standard is 2 years.
✗ 5 years — Exceeds the maximum contestability window; 2 years is the ceiling.

——————————
[Q 7 / 15 · Life Policy Provisions]
If a life insurance applicant understated their age, the death benefit will be:
A. Denied entirely
B. Paid in full as applied
C. Adjusted to what the premium would have bought at the correct age
D. Reduced by a 10% penalty
Answer: C. Adjusted to what the premium would have bought at the correct age
The misstatement of age provision adjusts the benefit to the amount the premium paid would have purchased at the correct age.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Denied entirely — Age misstatement is not fraud grounds for denial; the benefit is adjusted, not voided.
✗ Paid in full as applied — Because the premium bought less at the true age, the benefit is reduced accordingly.
✗ Reduced by a 10% penalty — There is no flat 10% penalty; the benefit is recomputed from what the premium would have purchased.

——————————
[Q 8 / 15 · Nonforfeiture Options]
Unless the owner elects otherwise, a lapsed whole life policy defaults to which nonforfeiture option?
A. Cash surrender value
B. Reduced paid-up insurance
C. Extended term insurance
D. Automatic premium loan
Answer: C. Extended term insurance
The default nonforfeiture option for a lapsed whole life policy is extended term insurance.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Cash surrender value — Taking cash surrender must be elected; it is not the automatic default.
✗ Reduced paid-up insurance — RPU is an available option but not the default; extended term is the default.
✗ Automatic premium loan — APL is a policy rider that must be selected, not the standard nonforfeiture default.

——————————
[Q 9 / 15 · Dividend Options]
Which dividend option generally produces the greatest long-term increase in death benefit and cash value?
A. Cash
B. Reduce premium
C. Accumulate at interest
D. Paid-up additions
Answer: D. Paid-up additions
Paid-up additions buy small fully paid-up insurance that grows tax-deferred and generates further dividends, usually producing the greatest long-term increase.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Cash — Taking dividends in cash removes them from the policy, adding nothing to death benefit or cash value.
✗ Reduce premium — Using dividends to lower premiums does not build additional coverage or cash value.
✗ Accumulate at interest — Accumulating grows cash value modestly but buys no additional insurance, so it lags paid-up additions.

——————————
[Q 10 / 15 · Life Insurance Tax]
How are MEC distributions (loans/withdrawals) generally taxed?
A. Tax-free up to basis (FIFO)
B. Ordinary income on a LIFO basis, with a 10% penalty before age 59½
C. Long-term capital gains
D. Always fully tax-free
Answer: B. Ordinary income on a LIFO basis, with a 10% penalty before age 59½
MEC distributions are taxed LIFO as ordinary income, with a 10% penalty if before age 59½. Non-MEC life insurance is taxed FIFO (tax-free up to basis).
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Tax-free up to basis (FIFO) — That is the treatment for non-MEC life insurance; MECs are taxed LIFO (gain first).
✗ Long-term capital gains — MEC gains are ordinary income, not capital gains.
✗ Always fully tax-free — Only basis is tax-free; MEC gain is taxable, plus a possible pre-59½ penalty.

——————————
[Q 11 / 15 · 1035 Exchange]
Which of the following is a PERMITTED tax-free Section 1035 exchange?
A. Annuity to life insurance
B. Life insurance to an annuity
C. Long-term care to life insurance
D. Annuity to endowment
Answer: B. Life insurance to an annuity
Life insurance may be exchanged tax-free into an annuity, but you cannot exchange an annuity or LTC contract into life insurance.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Annuity to life insurance — Not allowed — you cannot exchange an annuity into life insurance under 1035.
✗ Long-term care to life insurance — Not permitted; LTC can go to LTC or annuity, but not into life insurance.
✗ Annuity to endowment — Annuity cannot be exchanged into an endowment; the ladder only moves toward annuities/LTC.

——————————
[Q 12 / 15 · Joint Life]
A second-to-die (survivorship) policy is especially useful for:
A. Funding a buy-sell agreement at the first owner's death
B. Estate planning using the unlimited marital deduction
C. Covering a home mortgage
D. Short-term income replacement
Answer: B. Estate planning using the unlimited marital deduction
Second-to-die pays at the last death and is used in estate planning with the unlimited marital deduction. First-to-die is used to fund buy-sell agreements.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Funding a buy-sell agreement at the first owner's death — Buy-sell needs cash at the FIRST owner's death; that is first-to-die insurance. Survivorship pays only at the last death.
✗ Covering a home mortgage — A mortgage needs coverage at the first death; second-to-die pays only when both insureds die.
✗ Short-term income replacement — Survivorship pays at the last death, useless for immediate income needs — term fits that.

——————————
[Q 13 / 15 · Needs Analysis]
In a life insurance needs analysis, the two broad ECONOMIC assumptions the planner must set are:
A. Risk tolerance and current resources
B. Rate of return and inflation
C. Life expectancy and health status
D. Marginal tax bracket and state of residence
Answer: B. Rate of return and inflation
Rate of return and inflation are the broad economic assumptions. Risk tolerance and current resources are client attributes, not economic assumptions.

——————————
[Q 14 / 15 · MEC]
A modified endowment contract (MEC) can arise in each of the following EXCEPT:
A. Whole life
B. Universal life
C. Variable universal life
D. Term life
Answer: D. Term life
Only cash-value policies (whole life, UL, VUL) can become MECs. Term insurance has no cash-value capacity, so it can never be a MEC.

——————————
[Q 15 / 15 · Life Policy Provisions]
Which statement about life insurance beneficiary designations is FALSE?
A. A contingent beneficiary receives the proceeds only if the primary beneficiary predeceases the insured
B. Most beneficiary designations are irrevocable
C. There is no limit to the number of beneficiaries named in a class
D. A revocable designation can be changed by the owner without the beneficiary's consent
Answer: B. Most beneficiary designations are irrevocable
Most designations are REVOCABLE, so the owner may change them freely. An irrevocable designation requires the beneficiary's consent to change, but that is the exception, not the norm.



===== FP512 · M4 ANNUITIES =====

[7 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 7 · Annuities]
Which premium method most commonly funds a deferred annuity?
A. Single premium
B. Fixed premium
C. Flexible premium
D. Modal premium
Answer: C. Flexible premium
Flexible premium is the most common funding method for deferred annuities. Single premium most commonly funds immediate annuities.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Single premium — Single premium most commonly funds immediate annuities, not deferred ones.
✗ Fixed premium — Fixed scheduled premiums are not the common deferred-annuity structure; flexibility is the norm.
✗ Modal premium — Modal refers only to payment frequency, not a funding method for deferred annuities.

——————————
[Q 2 / 7 · Annuity Payout]
Which annuity payout option provides the maximum guaranteed monthly income for a given sum?
A. Joint and survivor
B. Life with 20-year period certain
C. Straight (pure) life
D. Refund annuity
Answer: C. Straight (pure) life
Straight (pure) life provides the maximum income but leaves nothing to a beneficiary. Joint and survivor provides the lowest income.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Joint and survivor — J&S covers two lives longer, so it pays the lowest income, not the highest.
✗ Life with 20-year period certain — Guaranteeing 20 years of payments lowers the monthly amount versus straight life.
✗ Refund annuity — Guaranteeing a refund of principal reduces the payout below straight life.

——————————
[Q 3 / 7 · Annuity Tax]
A nonqualified deferred annuity withdrawal is taxed:
A. As return of principal first, then earnings
B. As earnings (ordinary income) first on a LIFO basis
C. As long-term capital gain
D. Tax-free in all cases
Answer: B. As earnings (ordinary income) first on a LIFO basis
Nonqualified annuity withdrawals are taxed LIFO — earnings (ordinary income) come out first, then nontaxable return of principal. A 10% penalty applies to taxable amounts before age 59½.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ As return of principal first, then earnings — That is FIFO; nonqualified annuity withdrawals are LIFO (earnings out first).
✗ As long-term capital gain — Annuity earnings are ordinary income, never capital gain.
✗ Tax-free in all cases — Only the return-of-principal portion is tax-free; earnings are taxable.

——————————
[Q 4 / 7 · Annuity Tax]
The exclusion ratio for an annuitized payment equals:
A. Expected return divided by investment in the contract
B. Investment in the contract divided by total expected return
C. Investment in the contract divided by the annual payment
D. Earnings divided by basis
Answer: B. Investment in the contract divided by total expected return
Exclusion ratio = investment in the contract ÷ total expected return; it determines the nontaxable portion of each payment until basis is recovered.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Expected return divided by investment in the contract — The ratio is inverted — it is investment divided by expected return.
✗ Investment in the contract divided by the annual payment — That yields a number of years, not the tax-exclusion fraction.
✗ Earnings divided by basis — Wrong components entirely; the exclusion ratio uses basis over total expected return.

——————————
[Q 5 / 7 · Indexed Annuities]
Compared with an equity-indexed annuity (EIA), a registered index-linked annuity (RILA):
A. Has a higher guaranteed minimum rate
B. Cannot lose value
C. Has no guaranteed minimum rate, so the investor can lose money
D. Is not regulated by FINRA or the SEC
Answer: C. Has no guaranteed minimum rate, so the investor can lose money
Unlike an EIA (which has a guaranteed minimum rate and cannot lose value), a RILA has no guaranteed minimum rate; it uses a floor or buffer, so investors can lose money.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Has a higher guaranteed minimum rate — A RILA has NO guaranteed minimum rate; the EIA is the one with a floor guarantee.
✗ Cannot lose value — The EIA cannot lose value; a RILA can, via its buffer or floor structure.
✗ Is not regulated by FINRA or the SEC — RILAs are registered securities subject to SEC/FINRA oversight.

——————————
[Q 6 / 7 · Annuity Riders]
The most popular annuity living-benefit rider, selected by nearly 70% of buyers, is the:
A. Guaranteed Minimum Income Benefit (GMIB)
B. Guaranteed Minimum Accumulation Benefit (GMAB)
C. Guaranteed Lifetime Withdrawal Benefit (GLWB)
D. Guaranteed Minimum Withdrawal Benefit (GMWB)
Answer: C. Guaranteed Lifetime Withdrawal Benefit (GLWB)
The GLWB is the most popular rider, guaranteeing the right to withdraw a specified percentage each year for life.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Guaranteed Minimum Income Benefit (GMIB) — GMIB requires annuitization to access; it is far less popular than the GLWB.
✗ Guaranteed Minimum Accumulation Benefit (GMAB) — GMAB guarantees principal, not lifetime withdrawals, and is not the top seller.
✗ Guaranteed Minimum Withdrawal Benefit (GMWB) — GMWB guarantees withdrawals only until principal is recovered, not for life like the GLWB.

——————————
[Q 7 / 7 · Annuity Tax]
When a nonqualified deferred annuity is inherited, the gain in the contract is:
A. Stepped up to fair market value at the owner's death
B. Received income-tax-free by the beneficiary
C. Taxed as ordinary income to the beneficiary (income in respect of a decedent)
D. Taxed as long-term capital gain
Answer: C. Taxed as ordinary income to the beneficiary (income in respect of a decedent)
A non-annuitized annuity gets NO step-up in basis at death; the untaxed gain is income in respect of a decedent (IRD), taxed as ordinary income. A spouse may instead continue the contract; a non-spouse is generally subject to the 10-year rule.



===== FP512 · M5 HEALTH, MEDICARE & MEDICAID =====

[10 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 10 · COBRA]
How long must continuation coverage be offered after a divorce makes a spouse lose group health coverage?
A. 18 months
B. 29 months
C. 36 months
D. 12 months
Answer: C. 36 months
Divorce or legal separation is a 36-month COBRA qualifying event. Termination is 18 months; Social Security disability is 29 months.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 18 months — 18 months is the COBRA period for employment termination or hour reduction, not divorce.
✗ 29 months — 29 months applies to the Social Security disability extension, not divorce.
✗ 12 months — Not a COBRA period; divorce qualifies for 36 months.

——————————
[Q 2 / 10 · COBRA]
Which event is NOT a COBRA qualifying event?
A. Voluntary termination of employment
B. Reduction to part-time status
C. Termination for gross misconduct
D. Divorce from the covered employee
Answer: C. Termination for gross misconduct
Termination for gross misconduct is not a qualifying event; neither the employee nor dependents are eligible for COBRA.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Voluntary termination of employment — Voluntary termination (not for gross misconduct) is a qualifying event — 18 months.
✗ Reduction to part-time status — A reduction in hours causing loss of coverage is a qualifying event.
✗ Divorce from the covered employee — Divorce is a qualifying event giving the ex-spouse 36 months.

——————————
[Q 3 / 10 · ACA]
Under the ACA, dependent children may remain on a parent's health plan until age:
A. 18
B. 21
C. 26
D. 30
Answer: C. 26
The ACA requires dependent coverage to age 26, regardless of the child's tax-dependency or marital status.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 18 — Too low; the ACA extends coverage well beyond the age of majority.
✗ 21 — That is a common trust/support age, not the ACA dependent-coverage age.
✗ 30 — Exceeds the ACA limit; coverage ends at 26 regardless of marital or tax status.

——————————
[Q 4 / 10 · Health Plans]
Which managed care plan requires a primary care physician gatekeeper and generally provides no out-of-network coverage except emergencies?
A. PPO
B. HMO
C. Indemnity plan
D. POS plan
Answer: B. HMO
An HMO uses a PCP gatekeeper and covers only in-network care (except emergencies), typically with copays and no deductibles. A PPO allows out-of-network use at a lower rate.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ PPO — A PPO needs no gatekeeper and covers out-of-network care at a reduced rate.
✗ Indemnity plan — Indemnity (fee-for-service) plans have no network restrictions or gatekeeper at all.
✗ POS plan — A POS uses a gatekeeper but DOES allow out-of-network care (at higher cost), unlike an HMO.

——————————
[Q 5 / 10 · Medicaid]
The Medicaid lookback period for asset transfers is:
A. 12 months
B. 36 months
C. 60 months
D. No lookback applies
Answer: C. 60 months
Medicaid uses a 60-month (5-year) lookback. The ineligibility period equals the amount transferred divided by the monthly regional cost of nursing home care.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 12 months — Too short; Medicaid reviews transfers over a 60-month window.
✗ 36 months — 36 months was the old rule; the current lookback is 60 months.
✗ No lookback applies — A lookback definitely applies — five years for uncompensated transfers.

——————————
[Q 6 / 10 · Medicare]
Inpatient hospital and skilled nursing facility care are covered under which part of Medicare?
A. Part A
B. Part B
C. Part C
D. Part D
Answer: A. Part A
Part A covers inpatient hospital, skilled nursing facility, home health, and hospice. Part B covers physician/outpatient services; Part D covers prescription drugs.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Part B — Part B covers physician and outpatient services, not inpatient hospital/SNF stays.
✗ Part C — Part C (Medicare Advantage) bundles A and B through a private plan; it is not the base inpatient benefit.
✗ Part D — Part D covers prescription drugs only.

——————————
[Q 7 / 10 · Medicare]
The Medicare Initial Enrollment Period spans how many months around the 65th birthday?
A. 3 months
B. 6 months
C. 7 months
D. 8 months
Answer: C. 7 months
The Initial Enrollment Period is 7 months: the 3 months before the birth month, the birth month, and the 3 months after.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 3 months — Only the months before the birth month; the full IEP is longer.
✗ 6 months — Undercounts; the IEP is 7 months, not 6.
✗ 8 months — 8 months is the Special Enrollment Period after losing employer coverage, not the IEP.

——————————
[Q 8 / 10 · Medicare]
Under 2025 rules, Medicare Part A skilled nursing facility coverage pays in full for the first:
A. 100 days
B. 60 days
C. 20 days
D. 30 days
Answer: C. 20 days
After a qualifying 3-day hospital stay, Part A pays the first 20 days in full; days 21-100 carry daily coinsurance ($209.50 in 2025); after 100 days the patient pays all costs.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 100 days — 100 days is the maximum SNF benefit span, but days 21-100 require coinsurance — not paid in full.
✗ 60 days — 60 days is the full-coverage period for inpatient hospital, not SNF.
✗ 30 days — Incorrect figure; SNF full coverage is the first 20 days.

——————————
[Q 9 / 10 · Medicare]
How many standardized Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plans exist?
A. 4
B. 6
C. 10
D. 12
Answer: C. 10
There are 10 standardized Medigap plans (A-N). Plans F and G are the most popular; Plan F is limited to those eligible before 1/1/2020.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 4 — Too few; there are 10 lettered plans (A-N).
✗ 6 — Undercounts the standardized plan set of 10.
✗ 12 — Overcounts; only 10 standardized Medigap plans exist.

——————————
[Q 10 / 10 · Medicare Part D]
Starting in 2025, the Inflation Reduction Act caps annual out-of-pocket Medicare Part D drug costs at:
A. $590
B. $2,000
C. $8,000
D. No cap
Answer: B. $2,000
Beginning 2025, Part D out-of-pocket costs are capped at $2,000 (replacing the prior ~$8,000 limit) and the donut hole is eliminated.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ $590 — That is roughly the 2025 Part D deductible, not the out-of-pocket cap.
✗ $8,000 — $8,000 was the prior (pre-2025) threshold; the new cap is $2,000.
✗ No cap — The IRA specifically created a hard $2,000 annual cap.



===== FP512 · M6 DISABILITY, LTC & VETERANS BENEFITS =====

[8 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 8 · Disability Income]
Which definition of disability is the broadest and carries the highest premium?
A. Any occupation
B. Own occupation
C. Social Security definition
D. Loss of income
Answer: B. Own occupation
Own-occupation is the broadest definition (disabled if unable to perform one's own occupation) and has the highest premium. Any-occupation is the narrowest private definition.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Any occupation — Any-occ is the narrowest, cheapest definition — disabled only if unable to do any job.
✗ Social Security definition — The SSDI definition is very strict (any substantial gainful activity), the opposite of broad.
✗ Loss of income — An income-loss (loss-of-earnings) definition pays on income drop but is not the broadest own-occ standard.

——————————
[Q 2 / 8 · Disability Income]
If an employer pays the full premium for a group disability policy, the benefits received are:
A. Tax-free to the employee
B. Fully taxable to the employee
C. Taxed as capital gains
D. Tax-free up to 60% of income
Answer: B. Fully taxable to the employee
Employer-paid (or employee pretax-paid) disability benefits are taxable. If the employee pays with after-tax dollars, benefits are tax-free.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Tax-free to the employee — Benefits are tax-free only when the employee paid premiums with after-tax dollars.
✗ Taxed as capital gains — Disability benefits are ordinary income when taxable, not capital gains.
✗ Tax-free up to 60% of income — There is no 60%-of-income exclusion; employer-paid benefits are fully taxable.

——————————
[Q 3 / 8 · Disability Income]
A disability policy that is renewable for the full term AND whose premium cannot be changed is:
A. Guaranteed renewable
B. Conditionally renewable
C. Noncancelable
D. Optionally renewable
Answer: C. Noncancelable
Noncancelable policies guarantee both renewal and a fixed premium (most expensive). Guaranteed renewable allows premium changes for an entire class.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Guaranteed renewable — Guaranteed renewable locks renewal but the insurer CAN raise premiums for the whole class.
✗ Conditionally renewable — Renewal depends on stated conditions and premiums can change — weaker than noncancelable.
✗ Optionally renewable — The insurer chooses whether to renew, so neither renewal nor premium is guaranteed.

——————————
[Q 4 / 8 · Disability Income]
A residual disability benefit pays:
A. 50% of the benefit regardless of income loss
B. In proportion to the actual percentage of income lost
C. Only a lump sum at recovery
D. Nothing unless totally disabled
Answer: B. In proportion to the actual percentage of income lost
Residual benefits pay in proportion to actual income loss (40% income loss = 40% of benefit). A partial disability benefit instead pays a fixed portion regardless of income loss.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 50% of the benefit regardless of income loss — Residual pays proportionally to income lost, not a fixed 50%.
✗ Only a lump sum at recovery — Residual pays ongoing monthly benefits during partial disability, not a recovery lump sum.
✗ Nothing unless totally disabled — Residual specifically covers partial disability with actual income loss, not just total disability.

——————————
[Q 5 / 8 · Long-Term Care]
Under HIPAA, a tax-qualified LTC policy may pay benefits when the insured cannot perform at least how many ADLs?
A. 1 of 6
B. 2 of 6
C. 3 of 6
D. 4 of 6
Answer: B. 2 of 6
The HIPAA trigger is the inability to perform 2 or more of the 6 ADLs (for at least 90 days) OR cognitive impairment.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 1 of 6 — Too few; the trigger requires an inability to perform at least 2 of the 6 ADLs.
✗ 3 of 6 — Overstates the trigger — 2 ADLs, not 3, meets the HIPAA standard.
✗ 4 of 6 — Far above the standard; 2 ADLs (or cognitive impairment) is the trigger.

——————————
[Q 6 / 8 · Long-Term Care]
Which level of care does Medicare NOT cover?
A. Skilled nursing care
B. Intermediate care
C. Custodial care
D. Post-hospital home health
Answer: C. Custodial care
Medicare does not cover custodial (nonmedical, ADL-assistance) care, which is the most common type of LTC.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Skilled nursing care — Medicare does cover skilled nursing (post-hospital, limited days).
✗ Intermediate care — Intermediate skilled care can qualify; custodial care is the excluded type.
✗ Post-hospital home health — Medicare covers medically necessary post-hospital home health care.

——————————
[Q 7 / 8 · Long-Term Care]
The single most important LTC insurance rider is generally considered to be:
A. Return of premium
B. Inflation protection
C. Nonforfeiture
D. Restoration of benefits
Answer: B. Inflation protection
Inflation protection is the most important LTC rider and is required to be offered in many states; it may be compounding or simple.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Return of premium — ROP refunds premiums to a beneficiary but does nothing to protect benefit purchasing power.
✗ Nonforfeiture — Nonforfeiture preserves some value after lapse but is secondary to inflation protection.
✗ Restoration of benefits — Restoration restores used benefits after recovery — useful but not the top-ranked rider.

——————————
[Q 8 / 8 · Long-Term Care]
How are benefits from a tax-qualified LTC policy generally treated for income tax?
A. Fully taxable as ordinary income
B. Not taxable for qualified expenses, subject to a per diem limit
C. Taxed as capital gains
D. Taxed only above 7.5% of AGI
Answer: B. Not taxable for qualified expenses, subject to a per diem limit
Benefits for qualified expenses are not taxable, subject to a per diem limitation ($420 in 2025).
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Fully taxable as ordinary income — Qualified LTC benefits are generally tax-free, not fully taxable.
✗ Taxed as capital gains — LTC benefits are not investment gains; qualified benefits are simply excluded.
✗ Taxed only above 7.5% of AGI — The 7.5% AGI floor applies to the medical-expense deduction, not to LTC benefit taxation.



===== FP512 · M7 EMPLOYEE GROUP BENEFITS =====

[9 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 9 · Group Term Life]
Under Section 79, employer-provided group term life is tax-free to the employee up to what amount of coverage?
A. $25,000
B. $50,000
C. $100,000
D. $2,000
Answer: B. $50,000
The first $50,000 of employer-provided group term life is tax-free. Coverage above $50,000 is taxed using the Table I uniform-premium cost.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ $25,000 — Understates the threshold; the tax-free amount is $50,000 of coverage.
✗ $100,000 — Overstates it — coverage above $50,000 is taxed via Table I.
✗ $2,000 — That is a de minimis figure (e.g., dependent group life), not the $50,000 employee exclusion.

——————————
[Q 2 / 9 · Group Term Life]
A 52-year-old has $250,000 of employer-paid group term life. With a Table I rate of $0.23 per $1,000 per month, the annual imputed income is:
A. $276
B. $552
C. $690
D. $1,104
Answer: B. $552
[($250,000 - $50,000)/$1,000] × $0.23 × 12 = 200 × $0.23 × 12 = $552.

——————————
[Q 3 / 9 · Group Health]
Employer-paid group health insurance premiums are:
A. Taxable income to the employee and deductible to the employer
B. Deductible to the employer and not taxable to the employee
C. Nondeductible to the employer
D. Taxable to both parties
Answer: B. Deductible to the employer and not taxable to the employee
Employer-paid health premiums are a deductible business expense and are not taxable income to the employee.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Taxable income to the employee and deductible to the employer — Deductible to the employer is correct, but the premiums are NOT taxable to the employee.
✗ Nondeductible to the employer — Employer health premiums are an ordinary, deductible business expense.
✗ Taxable to both parties — Neither party is taxed — deductible to the employer, excluded for the employee.

——————————
[Q 4 / 9 · Self-Funded Plans]
A major advantage of a self-funded (ERISA) health plan is:
A. Guaranteed lower claims
B. Exemption from state benefit mandates and the state premium tax
C. No need for stop-loss insurance
D. State guaranty fund protection
Answer: B. Exemption from state benefit mandates and the state premium tax
ERISA exempts self-funded plans from state regulation, avoiding state-mandated benefits and the ~2% state premium tax. Stop-loss insurance is still typically purchased.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Guaranteed lower claims — Self-funding does not guarantee lower claims; the employer bears actual claim risk.
✗ No need for stop-loss insurance — Self-funded plans typically still buy stop-loss to cap catastrophic claims.
✗ State guaranty fund protection — ERISA plans are exempt from state regulation, so state guaranty funds do not protect them.

——————————
[Q 5 / 9 · HSA]
What is the 2025 maximum HSA contribution for family coverage (before catch-up)?
A. $4,300
B. $6,350
C. $8,300
D. $8,550
Answer: D. $8,550
The 2025 family HSA limit is $8,550 ($4,300 single); those 55+ may add a $1,000 catch-up.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ $4,300 — That is the 2025 single (self-only) HSA limit, not family.
✗ $6,350 — Not a current HSA figure; the 2025 family limit is $8,550.
✗ $8,300 — That was the 2024 family limit; 2025 rose to $8,550.

——————————
[Q 6 / 9 · Cafeteria Plans]
A Section 125 cafeteria plan must offer:
A. Only nontaxable benefits
B. A taxable cash option plus one or more qualified nontaxable benefits
C. Long-term care insurance
D. Educational assistance
Answer: B. A taxable cash option plus one or more qualified nontaxable benefits
A cafeteria plan must offer a taxable cash benefit plus at least one qualified nontaxable benefit. LTC insurance and educational assistance cannot be offered in it.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Only nontaxable benefits — A cafeteria plan must include a taxable cash choice, not solely nontaxable benefits.
✗ Long-term care insurance — LTC insurance is expressly prohibited inside a cafeteria plan.
✗ Educational assistance — Educational assistance cannot be offered through a Section 125 plan.

——————————
[Q 7 / 9 · FSA]
Regarding unused FSA balances, a plan may offer:
A. Both a grace period and a carryover
B. Either a grace period of up to 2½ months OR a carryover of up to $660 (2025), but not both
C. An unlimited rollover
D. A cash refund
Answer: B. Either a grace period of up to 2½ months OR a carryover of up to $660 (2025), but not both
A health FSA may offer either a grace period of up to 2½ months OR a carryover of up to $660 (2025) of unused funds, but not both.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Both a grace period and a carryover — A plan may offer one or the other, never both simultaneously.
✗ An unlimited rollover — Carryover is capped ($660 in 2025), not unlimited.
✗ A cash refund — Unused FSA funds are forfeited (use-it-or-lose-it), not refunded in cash.

——————————
[Q 8 / 9 · Workers' Compensation]
Workers' compensation insurance is funded by:
A. The employee through payroll deduction
B. The employer alone
C. Equally split between employer and employee
D. The state general fund
Answer: B. The employer alone
Workers' compensation is funded solely by the employer. Benefits for injury/sickness are excluded from the employee's income; it is a form of absolute liability.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ The employee through payroll deduction — Employees do not pay for workers' comp; the employer funds it entirely.
✗ Equally split between employer and employee — It is not shared — the employer bears the full cost.
✗ The state general fund — Employers (or their insurers/self-funding) pay, not the state general fund.

——————————
[Q 9 / 9 · Group Term Life]
A group term life carve-out plan typically removes which employees from the group plan into individual coverage?
A. Younger, lower-paid staff
B. Older, higher-paid executives
C. Part-time employees
D. New hires in their first year
Answer: B. Older, higher-paid executives
A carve-out moves older, higher-paid executives out of the group term plan into individual coverage. Nondiscrimination rules don't apply to the carve-out, which can bring the base plan into compliance; the coverage is taxable to the employee.



===== FP512 · M8 BUSINESS RISK SOLUTIONS =====

[6 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 6 · Key Person Insurance]
With key person life insurance, premiums and the death benefit are treated how?
A. Premiums deductible; death benefit taxable
B. Premiums not deductible; death benefit tax-free
C. Both deductible and taxable
D. Premiums deductible; death benefit tax-free
Answer: B. Premiums not deductible; death benefit tax-free
Premiums for key person insurance are not deductible, and the death benefit (received by the business) is income-tax free.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Premiums deductible; death benefit taxable — Neither part is right — premiums are nondeductible and the benefit is tax-free.
✗ Both deductible and taxable — Premiums are not deductible, and the death benefit is not taxable.
✗ Premiums deductible; death benefit tax-free — The death benefit is tax-free, but the premiums are NOT deductible.

——————————
[Q 2 / 6 · Buy-Sell Agreements]
A cross-purchase buy-sell agreement becomes inefficient primarily when:
A. There is only one owner
B. There are more than two owners
C. The business is a corporation
D. The owners are related
Answer: B. There are more than two owners
In a cross-purchase, each owner buys a policy on each other owner, which becomes inefficient with more than two owners. An entity-purchase agreement is easier to administer.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ There is only one owner — A single owner has no co-owner to buy from; cross-purchase presumes multiple owners.
✗ The business is a corporation — Entity type does not drive cross-purchase inefficiency; the number of owners does.
✗ The owners are related — Family relationship does not create the policy-count problem; having many owners does.

——————————
[Q 3 / 6 · Professional Liability]
Errors and omissions (E&O) insurance is most appropriate for which professionals?
A. Surgeons and dentists
B. Accountants, lawyers, and financial planners
C. Manufacturers
D. Truck drivers
Answer: B. Accountants, lawyers, and financial planners
E&O insurance covers financial harm (accountants, lawyers, insurance agents, financial planners). Malpractice insurance covers physical harm (physicians, surgeons, dentists).
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Surgeons and dentists — Physicians and dentists need malpractice (physical-harm) coverage, not E&O.
✗ Manufacturers — Manufacturers need product-liability coverage, not professional E&O.
✗ Truck drivers — Truckers need commercial auto/liability coverage, not professional E&O.

——————————
[Q 4 / 6 · Commercial Insurance]
The businessowners policy (BOP) is designed primarily for:
A. Large corporations
B. Smaller businesses
C. Government entities
D. Sole employees only
Answer: B. Smaller businesses
The BOP combines property and liability coverages for smaller businesses; the commercial package policy (CPP) serves larger companies.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Large corporations — Large firms use the commercial package policy (CPP), not the BOP.
✗ Government entities — The BOP targets small commercial businesses, not government bodies.
✗ Sole employees only — The BOP is defined by business size, not headcount of one; it serves small businesses generally.

——————————
[Q 5 / 6 · LIRP]
A Life Insurance Retirement Plan (LIRP) can be funded with all of the following EXCEPT:
A. Whole life insurance
B. Universal life insurance
C. Term life insurance
D. A cash value policy
Answer: C. Term life insurance
A LIRP requires a permanent (cash value) policy such as whole or universal life and cannot be funded with term life, which has no cash value.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Whole life insurance — Whole life builds cash value and is a valid LIRP funding vehicle.
✗ Universal life insurance — UL is permanent cash-value coverage, suitable for a LIRP.
✗ A cash value policy — Any permanent cash-value policy works for a LIRP; that is exactly what is required.

——————————
[Q 6 / 6 · Business Risk]
Employee embezzlement and forgery are covered by which type of commercial policy?
A. Cyber liability insurance
B. Fraud/crime (fidelity) insurance
C. Commercial general liability
D. Business interruption insurance
Answer: B. Fraud/crime (fidelity) insurance
Fraud/crime (fidelity) insurance covers employee or third-party dishonesty, embezzlement, and forgery. Cyber insurance is a distinct policy covering data breach, ransomware, and related business interruption.
